concept_name: Rate law and order of reaction
source_book: NCERT Chemistry Class 12 Ch.3 Chemical Kinetics (rate expression, rate constant, order of a reaction, initial-rate method) — scope only; teaching method, examples and anchors are first-principles (chemistry.md source rule)

real_world_anchor.primary: A glowing wooden splint barely smoulders in air, but pushed into pure oxygen it bursts into flame — the same reaction, roughly five times the oxygen concentration, dramatically faster. How much faster a reaction gets when a concentration changes is a number, and that number — the order — has to be measured.
real_world_anchor.secondary: A disinfectant diluted with water still kills germs — just more slowly. Halving the concentration cuts the rate by a factor you can only find by experiment.
real_world_anchor.why_it_matters: Both anchors are things a student has seen, and both pose exactly the question the sim answers with a measured factor rather than an assertion — the order is read off a box that was never told the rate law.

formulas.rate_law: rate = k[A]ˣ[B]ʸ — the orders x and y are measured, never read off the balanced equation's coefficients
formulas.order_definition: x = order with respect to A, y = order with respect to B; x + y = overall order
formulas.rate_constant_definition: k = fitted forward event rate ÷ (nA × nB), the concentration-independent factor in the rate law — read from readout E only, never from the equilibrium-K chip
formulas.initial_rate_method: order is measured by comparing the INITIAL rates of two separately seeded fresh runs — on the run-pair states (STATE_2/STATE_3/STATE_4/STATE_5) an averaged read over R=3 repeated 350 ms windows at the opening of each run, elsewhere a fitted chord over the opening window — never a ratio pinned to an earlier instant of the same run
formulas.concentration_basis_note: a rate comparison across a volume change (STATE_4's piston, STATE_10's V slider) uses the concentration basis; every fixed-volume state uses the count basis, which differs from concentration only by a constant area factor that cancels in any ratio
formulas.first_order_law: the reverse (breakup) reaction AB → A + B is order 1: rate = k′[AB]

tts_sentences.text_en: This box holds A and B reacting to make AB.
The rate law is rate equals k times A to the x, times B to the y.
We don't know x and y yet — they have to be measured.
Today, we measure them.

tts_sentences.text_en: Run one: A at ninety, B kept abundant, rate measured and kept.
Run two: A becomes four times as much, B unchanged.
The rate reads about four times run one's.
Order with respect to A is one.
It matches the coefficient only for this one-step reaction — hidden steps elsewhere would give a different order.

run 1's averaged rate (mean of 3 repeats) kept at ×1.00, run 2's averaged ratio read live — the focal (Rule 32e)

A stays abundant, B starts at ninety, kept.
Now B becomes four times as much, A stays put.
The rate again reads about four times run one's.
Order with respect to B is also one.

tts_sentences.text_en: Same particles, half the room — so both concentrations double at once.
The rate reads about four times run one's, not two.
In collision theory, crowding barely changed the fraction of collisions clearing the barrier.
That has not changed.
What changed is how many times A meets B, and doubling both multiplies it by four.

misconception_watch.belief: Anything that adds collisions speeds the reaction.
misconception_watch.visual_counter: the collision counter reads clearly higher after the inert pour, while the initial-rate ratio chip still lands at about ×1.00
misconception_watch.one_line_fix: Only species named in the rate law change the rate — more collisions overall is not enough.

tts_sentences.text_en: Same test — but this time we pour in ninety inert grey particles, not more reactant.
The collision counter climbs: many more hits per second.
But the rate barely moves.
Particles the rate law doesn't name don't change the rate, even when they fill the box.

tts_sentences.text_en: Watch the rate bar shrink as A and B run out.
Now watch k.
It doesn't fall with the rate — it stays in the same rough range the whole time.
k is the part of the law that concentration does not change.

tts_sentences.text_en: Every few seconds this plots one point: the rate right now, against A times B right now.
The points land on one straight line through the origin — that is what order one in each looks like.
Its slope is k.
Pour in more A, and the new points land on the same line.

Now we plot the breakup rate against how much AB is left.
Again a straight line through the origin — but a different line, a different slope.
Breaking apart is order one: a different law from the one that built it.

entries.syllabus_unit: Class 12 Chemistry — Unit 3 Chemical Kinetics (rate law, order of reaction, rate constant, initial-rate method)
Physical Chemistry — Chemical Kinetics (rate law and order of reaction)
Reaction kinetics — orders of reaction, rate equations, rate constants
Reactivity 2.2 — What are the mechanisms of chemical change? (rate expressions)
Unit 5 — Kinetics (rate law, reaction order, rate constant)
Rate law / order of reaction is not part of the IGCSE Chemistry syllabus (qualitative rate factors only) — claimed, hidden at catalog level via the igcse preset, not by ring-cutting

assessment.mastery_definition: A student who can state what 'order with respect to a reactant' means, correctly predict the rate-factor from a stated concentration change (doubling one reactant, doubling both via volume, or adding an inert species), distinguish the rate constant k from the rate itself, explain why order is measured from initial rates on fresh mixtures rather than a running reaction, and read k as a straight line's slope on a rate-vs-concentration plot has mastered this concept.

questions.stem: In the rate law rate = k[A]ˣ[B]ʸ, the order with respect to A is found to be x = 1. What does that mean?

options.A: Doubling the concentration of A alone doubles the initial rate.
options.B: The balanced equation has one A on the reactant side, so x must equal 1.
options.C: A is completely used up in exactly one second.
options.D: The concentration of A stays constant throughout the reaction.

distractor_misconceptions.B: The coefficients in the balanced equation give the orders x and y — the central misconception this concept confronts.
distractor_misconceptions.C: Confuses the kinetic order with a literal consumption rate of one unit per second.
distractor_misconceptions.D: Confuses 'order one' with 'A is held constant' rather than 'the rate scales linearly with A'.

questions.parallel_form_stem: A student is told the order with respect to a reactant Q is one. What should happen to the initial rate if [Q] is doubled while everything else is held fixed?

questions.stem: In a fresh run, doubling [B] while holding [A] fixed makes the initial rate exactly double. What can you conclude about the order with respect to B?

options.A: Order with respect to B is 1.
options.B: Order with respect to B is 2, because rate and concentration both changed.
options.C: Order with respect to B is 0, because B's coefficient in the equation is 1.
options.D: The order cannot be found without knowing the order with respect to A first.

distractor_misconceptions.B: Mistakes 'the rate doubled' for 'the rate quadrupled' — confuses order 1 with order 2.
distractor_misconceptions.C: Reads the coefficient off the balanced equation instead of the measured doubling response — the central misconception.
distractor_misconceptions.D: Wrongly assumes orders with respect to different reactants are not independently measurable.

questions.parallel_form_stem: Doubling [A] while [B] is held fixed makes the initial rate four times larger. What is the order with respect to A?

questions.stem: The volume of a reaction vessel is halved at constant temperature, so both [A] and [B] double. If the reaction is order 1 in each reactant, by what factor does the rate change?

options.C: ×1 (no change, since only volume changed, not amounts)

distractor_misconceptions.B: Only accounts for ONE concentration doubling, missing that both double together.
distractor_misconceptions.C: Confuses particle count (unchanged) with concentration (which doubles when volume halves).
distractor_misconceptions.D: Over-multiplies — mistakes order (1+1=2, giving ×2²=×4) for a cubic dependence.

questions.parallel_form_stem: A gas-phase reaction is order 1 in A and order 1 in B. If the container's volume is reduced to one third, by what factor does the initial rate increase?

questions.stem: Ninety inert particles (which do not appear in the rate law) are added to a reaction mixture. What happens to the initial rate?

options.A: The rate stays about the same, even though total collisions per second rise.
options.B: The rate roughly doubles, since there are now more particles in the box.
options.C: The rate drops to zero, since the inert particles block reactant collisions completely.
options.D: The rate rises in proportion to the square of the number of inert particles added.

distractor_misconceptions.B: Assumes 'more particles anywhere in the box' automatically means 'more reaction' — ignores that only species in the rate law matter.
distractor_misconceptions.C: Overcorrects — assumes inert crowding stops the reaction rather than leaving it unchanged.
distractor_misconceptions.D: Invents a scaling law with no basis in the rate expression.

questions.parallel_form_stem: An inert gas is bled into a reacting mixture until the total pressure has risen sharply. Does the reaction rate rise by the same proportion?

questions.stem: As a reaction runs, the concentrations of A and B fall and the measured rate falls with them. What happens to the rate constant k over the same time, at constant temperature?

options.A: k stays in the same rough range — it does not track the falling rate.
options.B: k falls along with the rate, since rate = k[A][B].
options.C: k rises to compensate for the falling concentrations.
options.D: k is only defined at the instant the reaction starts, so the question has no meaning later on.

distractor_misconceptions.B: Confuses the rate (which depends on concentration) with the rate constant (which does not) — the central k-vs-rate misconception.
distractor_misconceptions.C: Invents a compensating mechanism that has no physical basis.
distractor_misconceptions.D: Wrongly assumes k is only meaningful at t = 0.

questions.parallel_form_stem: The same reaction mixture is heated from 300 K to 450 K, with concentrations unchanged at the moment of heating. What happens to k?

questions.stem: Why is a reaction's order measured from the initial rate of two freshly seeded experiments, rather than from a live rate measured partway through a single running reaction?

options.A: Because a running mixture may already contain product and a reverse reaction, which can make the same doubling test read the wrong exponent.
options.B: Because the initial rate is always the fastest rate a reaction ever reaches.
options.C: Because concentrations cannot be measured accurately once a reaction has started.
options.D: Because only the initial rate has correct units of concentration per second.

distractor_misconceptions.B: Confuses 'initial' with 'fastest' — for some reactions the initial rate is not the peak rate.
distractor_misconceptions.C: Concentration is measurable mid-reaction; that is not why initial rates are preferred here.
distractor_misconceptions.D: Units of rate do not depend on which point in the reaction is measured.

questions.parallel_form_stem: Two students measure the same reaction's rate response to doubling A — one on a fresh mixture, one on a mixture that has been running for a while with the reverse reaction active. Whose result correctly gives the order?

questions.stem: On a graph of forward rate (y) against A×B (x), the points lie on one straight line through the origin. What does the slope of that line represent?

options.B: The overall order of the reaction.
options.D: The activation energy of the reaction.

distractor_misconceptions.B: Confuses the slope (which reads off k) with the order (which is shown by the line being straight, not by its steepness).
distractor_misconceptions.C: Confuses a graph slope with an axis intercept or a starting value.
distractor_misconceptions.D: Activation energy is read from a completely different plot (Arrhenius), not a rate-vs-concentration line.

questions.parallel_form_stem: A different reaction's breakup rate is plotted against the amount of AB remaining, and the points also fall on one straight line through the origin. What does that line's slope represent for this reaction?

authoring_notes.s4_construction_critical: STATE_4's piston beat uses the EXACT measured construction from the chemistry block — do not simplify. A naive kinetics_reseed_charge.piston_frac springs back toward the state's OWN authored piston_frac at 6%/tick (gasMovePiston's free ease), landing back near 1.0 inside the fit window and reading a ratio far below ~4. The fix routes the stroke through the DRIVEN ramp branch: piston_from:1.0 + piston_frac:0.5 + piston_ramp_ms:60 + piston_cue set to the SAME id as kinetics_reseed_cue. There is deliberately NO settle gap between the cue and run 2's fit window (gap 0 measured ×4.23 concentration-basis; gap 1600 ms measured only ×2.81, because the reaction never pauses and keeps consuming reactant while waiting — waiting costs more than the area overshoot it fixes). kinetics_rate_basis:'concentration' is REQUIRED on this state (and on STATE_10's V slider) — the count-basis rate is a 2D collision-count rate ⎄ N_A·N_B/Area (an event rate), while the textbook concentration rate d[A]/dt ⎄ N_A·N_B/Area² carries one extra factor of area; without the concentration basis this state would read ~×2 under a caption claiming ×4. STATE_4's species_counts/kinetics_reseed_charge are UNCHANGED by the 2026-08 recalibration. Its window/R WAS briefly aligned to the other run-pair states' 350 ms/R=3 discipline and that alignment is now REVERTED — that setting was measured for the pour-based charge on STATE_2/STATE_3/STATE_5, never for this piston state, and running it on STATE_4 read ×0.64 (a 36% DECREASE) at t=5000-19000 ms against a title/caption/narration all claiming ×4 (scar: calibration_discipline_propagated_to_a_state_whose_measurement_did_not_cover_it). STATE_4 is restored to the window ITS OWN measurement covers: kinetics_window_ms:2000, kinetics_repeat_runs omitted (R=1 — the 40-seed ratio-of-sums held 3.87-4.23, and 3.37-4.13 at design.phys_seed 29919362, both measured at R=1/2000 ms, never at 350 ms/R=3). The reseed cue's at_ms is recomputed off the restored window, not left at the 350 ms/R=3 value: R x window = 1 x 2000 = 2000 ms; at_ms:3500 clears that by a 1500 ms margin, above this concept's own measured 1300 ms floor for this guard (see kinetics_repeat_run_discipline) with a similar buffer to the other run-pair states' 1450 ms-over-1300 ms margin. kinetics_marks follow: open [0,2000] keep:true, cue [3500,5500] at_cue:'reseed' — no settle gap preserved (cue mark t0 === cue at_ms, per the no-gap measurement above). STATE_4's dwell (duration 19 s / eye_capture_ms 19000) already clears the new cue window's end (5500 ms) with 13500 ms to spare for the piston stroke, the read beat and the narration — comparable to or larger than the other run-pair states' post-cue-window headroom (9150-14650 ms) — so neither field needed to grow.
authoring_notes.kinetics_repeat_run_discipline: STATE_2/STATE_3/STATE_5 author kinetics_window_ms:350 + kinetics_repeat_runs:3 (R=3 x 350 ms = 1050 ms per slot, both the 'open' mark and the 'cue' mark) — this discipline was measured for the pour-based run-pair states' raised-B/raised-A charge only. Each of those three states' reseed cue fires at_ms:2500, which clears the engine's guard against the cue arming while the 'open' slot's own repeat sequence is still mid-flight (particle_field_renderer.ts ~4149-4174 — firing too early silently falls back to a single-shot reseed, degrading the read to R=1) with margin 2500-1050=1450 ms, above the measured 1300 ms floor. STATE_4 (the piston state) does NOT share this discipline — its own measurement covers a 2000 ms window at R=1, not 350 ms/R=3; applying the 350 ms/R=3 setting to STATE_4 is the exact regression this pass reverted (see s4_construction_critical). STATE_4's kinetics_repeat_runs is therefore omitted (R=1, byte-identical to authoring the value 1) and its reseed cue at_ms:3500 clears its OWN R x window (1 x 2000 = 2000 ms) by 1500 ms, above the same measured 1300 ms floor used above — the floor is a property of the engine's cue-vs-window-close guard, not of the 350 ms/R=3 setting specifically, so it is reused rather than re-derived. (The old STATE_8's separate single-shot 2500 ms window construction is gone with that state — see state8_removed_named_fallback.)

DQ-2 has now definitively failed: with the concept's run-pair states re-calibrated to quadrupling (see measured_constants), S8's home-box-run-partway charge family A(90−n)/B(90−n)/AB(n) was swept across 40+ configurations — baseline Ea 3/reverse 8 and Ea 3/reverse 8 alternates, AB charge n from 10 to 200, fit windows 350/700/1000 ms, repeat counts R from 3 to 20 — and in every configuration the doubled-A net-rate ratio either overlapped the fresh-box ×4 reference in both independent measurement batches (no separable signal) or diverged wildly on a near-zero net baseline (individual seeds reading −962, 374, 188 — the box sitting too close to equilibrium for an initial-rate measurement to be well-posed at all). The cause is structural, not a tuning miss: the forward step scales with N_A·N_B while the reverse step is first-order in AB alone, so a large seeded B dominates the net rate unless AB is pushed to where the box is genuinely near equilibrium — exactly where 'initial rate' stops being a well-defined quantity. Depletion itself was fine throughout (3.9–5.0%, inside the <=10% bound); the signal could not be made simultaneously large and stable.
